rich_text.plain_text: There's a long Norwegian precedent for that attitude to a flower. Rosemaling, the decorative painting that flourished from the 1700s to the mid-1800s in valleys such as Hallingdal and Telemark, is built on fantasy flowers: blooms so stylised that no specific flower is identifiable, laid out with scrollwork across ale bowls, cupboards, trunks and church interiors. The aim was ornament, not accuracy.

rich_text.plain_text: Paper cutting has its own Nordic lineage. Hans Christian Andersen was a serious practitioner, cutting figures while he improvised stories for party guests and handing the result over at the end of the tale. About a thousand of them still exist, on the count of the Royal Danish Library, which holds two of the collections itself. Smaller figures do the rounds, but they tend to be one museum's holdings rather than the total. The technique forces a decision a botanical plate never has to make: with one tone and one cut edge you can't describe a leaf, only its shape. Brox's branches work the same way, and it's why the print settles a bedroom or a reading corner instead of demanding attention from it.
